_comment: What each capability name MEANS. Until this file existed the names in
was given a vocabulary and no definitions, so recognising a deletion
rested entirely on the model's prior for the English word. Everything
downstream then treated the label as fact — a mislabelled region becomes
a high-severity finding about the application rather than a bad guess.
`signals` and `excludes` are evidence to weigh, not a checklist. The
graph the classifier reads holds control labels, routes and transitions,
so every signal is written in those terms and nothing here asks about
page content the model was never shown.
`supported: false` means the rule base has no invariant for this
capability yet. Such a candidate is still worth proposing: it is
reported as a named coverage gap instead of disappearing, which is the
whole difference between 'we did not test this' and silence.

create_resource.definition: A user brings a new resource into existence, and it is afterwards addressable in its own right.
signals: a control labelled New/Add/Create leading to a form route such as /things/new
submitting that form lands on a detail route for an instance that did not previously exist
the collection it returns to gains a row
excludes: adding an item to a cart or basket — that mutates one existing resource rather than creating an addressable one
a form that edits something already present (that is update_resource)
sign-up, which creates a session as well and is authenticate
create_resource.outcome: The new resource's own URL answers after the flow, so the probe is `final`.

update_resource.definition: A user changes a field of an existing resource and the change is expected to persist.
signals: an Edit control on a resource detail route leading to a form pre-filled with that resource's current values
a Save/Update control returning to the same resource
excludes: a form that creates something new
view state that is not written back — sorting, filtering, collapsing a sidebar
update_resource.outcome: The changed value is readable on the resource after the flow.
update_resource.gap: No flow invariant asserts this yet. The page-level persistence invariants cover the single-page version of the same idea; they cannot follow a commit that navigates.

delete_resource.definition: A user permanently removes a resource, and it stops existing — not merely stops being listed.
signals: a Delete/Remove/Destroy control on a resource's own detail route
the flow returns to the collection the resource belonged to
the collection has one fewer row afterwards
excludes: archiving, disabling, deactivating, cancelling or marking something inactive — the row disappears but the resource is meant to survive, so the deletion assertion would be wrong
removing a line from a cart or a list that is itself one editable resource
clearing filters or a search, which removes rows from a view and nothing from the application
delete_resource.outcome: The resource's own URL must stop answering, which is why this needs a `captured` probe taken before the deletion.

authenticate.definition: A user establishes a session by proving who they are.
signals: a login route with credential fields and a Sign in / Log in control
the flow lands somewhere only a signed-in user reaches
excludes: signing out (that is session_termination)
a form that merely collects contact details during checkout
authenticate.outcome: Evidence the session is active is readable after the flow.
authenticate.gap: No flow invariant asserts this yet. Candidates are reported as a coverage gap. Note the crawler already signs in via --credential to reach authenticated states, so this capability is about *asserting* the sign-in, not about reaching the pages behind it.

session_termination.definition: A user ends their session, and access that depended on it stops working.
signals: a Sign out / Log out control, usually on an account or profile route
the flow returns to a login or public landing route
excludes: navigating away from an account page while still signed in
switching accounts or profiles without dropping the session
session_termination.outcome: A protected path must stop being reachable, so this needs a `path` probe naming one. A page that answers 200 by redirecting to a login screen is NOT reachable for this purpose — the probe compares the answering path with the requested one.

sort_collection.definition: A user reorders a collection by a column it displays, without changing which rows are in it.
signals: a sort control, or a sort parameter appearing in the route
the same rows appear in a different order afterwards
the ordered column is numeric or a date, so an ordering can actually be checked
excludes: filtering or searching, which changes which rows are present (that is filter_collection)
pagination
a sort over a column with no order to verify, such as free text
sort_collection.outcome: The sorted column's values, in displayed order, must be non-decreasing. Read them as numbers: a sort applied to the rendered string is exactly the defect this catches, and reading strings back would reproduce the bug rather than detect it.

filter_collection.definition: A user narrows a collection to a subset, and the page both displays and states how many rows remain.
signals: a filter or search control whose submission adds query parameters to the route
the page states a count alongside the rows it shows
excludes: sorting, which reorders without narrowing
a filter whose result page states no count — there is then nothing for the collection-count invariant to compare against
filter_collection.outcome: The stated count and the displayed row count must agree.

search.definition: A user queries a collection by free text and is shown matches.
signals: a search field whose submission puts a query term in the route
results that vary with the term
excludes: a faceted filter with fixed options, which is filter_collection
search.outcome: Results correspond to the term searched for.
search.gap: No flow invariant asserts this yet, and relevance is not mechanically checkable the way a count or an ordering is. When a search page states a result count, prefer filter_collection, which can be checked.

multi_step_transaction.definition: A user completes a purchase or submission across several pages, ending on a confirmation that itemises what was committed and totals it.
signals: a sequence of routes under a common prefix such as /checkout/*
a terminal Place order / Submit / Confirm control
a confirmation page listing individual amounts and a grand total
excludes: a single-page form with no itemised total
the cart itself, which is the setup for this capability rather than the capability
multi_step_transaction.outcome: The individual line amounts must sum to the stated grand total. The capability is a reachability claim, not a fixed path: an optional upsell step appearing between runs leaves it intact.
